removed.text: She wears a wreath of cornflowers on her head.
removed.reason: machal1918:p.267 describes the Polish poludnica as a tall woman in a white robe with a sickle; it says nothing of a wreath of cornflowers, and a find for 'cornflower' and 'wreath' in machal1918 turned up no page saying it of her.

removed.text: When she leaves the fields or the forests she is accompanied by seven great black dogs.
removed.reason: Misplaced, belongs in behavior_habitat: being accompanied by seven black dogs when she leaves the fields is sourced on machal1918:p.268 but is not a physical description of her.

downgraded.text: Afanasyev derives the name poludnitsy from polden', noon, which he also glosses as the south, the warm, summer side.
downgraded.to_text: Afanasyev derives the name poludnitsy from polden', which he glosses as the south, the warm, summer side.
downgraded.reason: afanasyev1869:p.137 glosses полдень only as 'юг, теплая, летняя сторона' (south, warm, summer side); the gloss 'noon' is the drafter's, so it was cut.

flagged.reason: Printed so on machal1918:p.267, but the same line prints 'Pofudnica' for Poludnica, so 't' is probably OCR for 'ł' (Południowka); kept as printed.

flagged.text: In the same passage Afanasyev notes that priestless Old Believers say a prayer at noon to drive out "the noonday demon".
flagged.reason: afanasyev1869:p.138 places the Old Believers' noon prayer against 'бес полуденный' directly after the Archangel poludnitsa sayings but does not say the noonday demon is the poludnitsa; the tie is by juxtaposition only.

erben1893:p.183 says 'dle podání lidu' (according to folk tradition) without naming the Czechs; the people is fixed only by context (a Czech author's Czech collection). The same applies to the 'Czech folk tradition' wording in /scene/3 and /dealing_with_it/3.

grade_rationale.text: Machal records the poludnitsa for Bohemian (Czech) and Moravian tradition, for the Poles, for the Lusatian Serbs and for the Russians, including the Siberian Russians.
Afanasyev independently records her among the Czechs, the Lusatians and the Russians of the Archangel Government and southern Siberia.
Ralston records the Lusatian Prezpolnica or Pripolnica with her sickle and flax questions, and on this passage he cites neither Afanasyev nor Machal, so he counts as a third independent author.
Afanasyev's three citing volumes (1865, 1869) count as one source; Machal gives no source for these pages.
Erben's note on Czech folk tradition is a commentary in a literary collection and is not counted as an independent folklore source; the grade does not rest on it.
